html:
Persia was the name the West used for Iran until 1935, when the government asked foreign countries to use the name Iran. On the map it appears in 400 CE, under the Sasanian Empire, and from 1783 to 1914, under the Zand and then the Qajar shahs.

The name comes from Pars, the homeland in southwest Iran of the Achaemenid kings, whose empire under Cyrus the Great was the largest the world had seen. In 400 CE the Sasanians ruled from Ctesiphon in Iraq; they were the great rival of Rome and Byzantium, and their state religion was Zoroastrianism. After the Arab conquest Iran became Muslim but kept its language, and the Safavids made it Shia from 1501.

In the later snapshots Persia is the kingdom of the Qajar dynasty, with Tehran as its capital from 1786. It lost the Caucasus to Russia in wars in the early 1800s, and it fell under the rival pressure of Russia and Britain, which split it into zones of influence in 1907. The Constitutional Revolution of 1905 to 1911 gave it a parliament. In 1925 Reza Khan replaced the Qajars with his own Pahlavi dynasty.
